name: Reset your password
description: Sent the moment someone asks to reset a password: one time-boxed link, the raw URL underneath it, and nothing else competing for the click.

origin.note: Design: stark utility — square corners, no accent colour, no social chrome, the greeting demoted above the headline so the message reads as one instruction.

subject: Reset your {{ product.name }} password
preheader: Good for {{ expires_in }} and one use. Ignore it and nothing changes.

user.first_name.description: Recipient's first name. Absent for accounts that never collected one, which is common on password reset — the design drops the greeting rather than guessing.

heading_text.description: The headline. Keep it to the instruction itself: this email is scanned, not read.

body.description: The single explanatory sentence. Say what was asked for, so a recipient who did not ask knows immediately that something is off.
body.default: You asked to set a new password. Open the link below and choose one.

reset_url.description: The one-time reset link. It carries the token, so it is also printed in full underneath the button for clients that strip or rewrite it.

button_label.description: Label on the only action in the message. Name the outcome, not the mechanism.

fallback_note.description: Introduces the printed URL. Security gateways routinely rewrite or break buttons, and a reset with no visible link is a dead end.
fallback_note.default: If the button does not work, paste this into your browser:

expires_in.description: How long the link stays valid, stated as a duration because the recipient is reading this within minutes of asking for it.

expiry_note.description: What happens after a single use. Worth saying: people forward these to a second device and then wonder why the link is dead.
expiry_note.default: It stops working as soon as it is used once.

not_you_note.description: The line for the recipient who did not ask. It has to reassure and advise in the same breath, because a stream of unrequested resets is itself a signal.
not_you_note.default: Didn't ask for this? Ignore this email and your password stays as it is. If these keep arriving, someone knows your address — turning on two-factor authentication will stop them getting further.
